indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.3.1: Know that movement is caused by applied forces due to the release of stored energy
indicator.objective: Discover the effects of forces on objects

skills.description: Describe the effects of forces on objects (making them move, stopping them, changing shape, changing direction, changing speed)
Identify everyday actions that apply force to an object
Demonstrate a force changing the shape, movement, or direction of an object
Explain simply why an object moved, stopped, or changed shape

misconceptions: Forces only make things move; they cannot change shape.
If an object stops, no force was involved.
Pushing and pulling are the only forces.
A moving object has no force acting on it.

questions.stem: What happens to a ball when you kick it?
hints: You use your foot to push it.
questions.explanation: Kicking a ball applies a force that makes the ball move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think kicking only changes the shape of the ball.

questions.stem: When you squeeze a sponge, what happens to its shape?
hints: You press it with your hands.
questions.explanation: Squeezing applies a force that changes the shape of the sponge.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think forces only cause movement, not shape changes.

questions.stem: Which of these actions applies a force to an object?
questions.explanation: Pushing a wheelbarrow applies a force that moves it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think looking at an object applies a force.

questions.stem: Which action involves pulling?
hints: You drag it along the ground.
questions.explanation: Dragging a bag involves pulling it towards you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse pulling with pushing.

questions.stem: What happens to a moving toy car when you put your hand in front of it?
questions.explanation: Your hand applies a force that stops the moving toy car.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the car will go through the hand.

questions.stem: Ama squeezes a tube of toothpaste. What effect does her force have?
options: It changes the shape of the tube
It changes the colour of the tube
questions.explanation: Squeezing applies a force that changes the shape of the tube.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think squeezing changes the temperature.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a force changing the direction of a moving object?
options: Kicking a moving ball to the left
hints: You change where it is going.
questions.explanation: Kicking a moving ball to the left changes its direction.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize forces can change direction, not just start movement.

questions.stem: Kwame pushes a box on the floor. It starts to move. What effect did his push have?
questions.explanation: Kwame's push applied a force that made the stationary box move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you have to pull to make something move.

questions.stem: Which of these actions does NOT apply a force?
hints: Which action only uses your eyes?
questions.explanation: Watching a bird does not apply a force because you are not pushing or pulling anything.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeing something applies a force.

questions.stem: Why does a rolling ball eventually stop on its own?
options: Because the ground applies a friction force that slows it down
hints: The ground is not perfectly smooth.
There is rubbing between the ball and the floor.
questions.explanation: The ball stops because friction (a force from the ground and air) slows it down.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the ball stops because it runs out of energy completely.

questions.stem: Ama pushes a door, but it does not move. Why?
options: She is not applying a force
The door is too heavy or locked and resists her force
She is pulling instead of pushing
questions.explanation: The door does not move because another force (like friction or a lock) is pushing back against Ama's force. If the door is just too heavy, her force is not enough to overcome it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think no movement means no force was applied.

questions.stem: What happens to the shape of a rubber band when you stretch it?
hints: You pull it from both ends.
questions.explanation: Stretching applies a force that changes the shape of the rubber band, making it longer.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the rubber band breaks immediately.

questions.stem: Name one action that involves pushing an object.
hints: You move it away from you.
questions.explanation: Pushing a door or a box applies a force away from you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a pulling action.

questions.stem: Kofi is playing with a lump of clay. He presses it with his thumb. What effect does his force have?
options: It changes the shape of the clay
It turns the clay into stone
questions.explanation: The force from Kofi's thumb changes the shape of the clay.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not associate force with changing the shape of soft materials.

questions.stem: Why is it easier to move a chair by pushing it on a smooth floor than on a rough, sandy floor?
options: Because the chair is lighter on smooth floors
Because there is less friction force on the smooth floor
Because sand helps the chair move faster
hints: Think about rubbing your hands on sand.
questions.explanation: There is less friction (a resisting force) on a smooth floor, so it is easier to push the chair.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the chair changes weight.

questions.stem: Ama throws a ball up into the air. What force causes the ball to fall back down to the ground?
hints: It pulls things towards the Earth.
questions.explanation: Gravity is the force that pulls the ball back down to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wind blows it down.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how you can use a force to change the shape of a piece of paper.

criteria.description: Performs an action that changes the shape of the paper (e.g., crumpling, folding, tearing)
Explains that they applied a force

questions.explanation: Crushing or folding the paper applies a force that changes its shape.

questions.stem: Explain why a moving bicycle slows down when the rider applies the brakes.

criteria.description: States that the brakes apply a force
States that this force causes the bicycle to slow down or stop

hints: What do the brakes do to the wheel?
They stop the wheel from turning.
questions.explanation: The brakes apply a friction force to the wheels, which slows down and eventually stops the bicycle.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how you can use a force to change the direction of a moving object.

criteria.description: Performs an action that changes direction (e.g., hitting a ball to the side)
Explains that they applied a force

hints: Roll a ball and hit it with a stick.
Kick a ball slightly to the side.
questions.explanation: Hitting or kicking a moving ball to the side applies a force that changes its direction.

questions.stem: A car is moving fast. The driver applies the brakes hard. What happens to the car and why?
options: It speeds up because of the force
It stops because the brakes apply a force opposing the motion
It changes colour because of heat
questions.explanation: The brakes apply a force that opposes the car's movement, causing it to slow down and stop.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stopping requires no force.
